The Gap Between Demo and Production Is Where Most Projects Die

A multi-agent system that works in a Jupyter notebook is not a product. It is a hypothesis. The distance between that hypothesis and a system running reliably under real load — with observable state, recoverable failures, and defensible security posture — is where the majority of AI agent projects stop. Not because the underlying models are wrong, or because the use case lacks value, but because the engineering decisions made in the prototype phase are incompatible with production requirements, and nobody identified that incompatibility early enough to correct it.

This article describes the specific failure modes that stall agent projects before they ship, and the architectural decisions that distinguish systems that reach production from those that don't.

Failure Mode 1: State Is Stored in Memory, Not in a Durable Store

The fastest way to build an agent demo is to hold conversation history, task state, and intermediate results in process memory. It works perfectly until the process restarts — which in a Kubernetes environment happens constantly: rolling deployments, node evictions, resource pressure, liveness probe failures. When state lives in memory, every restart is a silent data loss event.

Production agent systems require a durable state store that survives process restarts and horizontal scaling. Postgres is the right default for most workloads: it handles structured agent state, supports transactional updates, and its JSON and JSONB column types accommodate the semi-structured payloads that multi-agent systems produce. The schema design matters significantly — agent task records need status fields with constrained enumerations, timestamps for created/updated/completed, parent-task foreign keys for hierarchical orchestration, and indexed columns on status and agent_id to support the polling patterns that orchestrator agents use.

The teams that ship production systems design the Postgres schema before they write the first agent. The teams that stall design it after, when they discover that migrating live state from in-memory structures to a relational store is a rewrite, not a refactor.

Failure Mode 2: Agents Communicate Synchronously Across Service Boundaries

Direct HTTP calls between agents feel natural in development. Service A calls Service B, waits for a response, and proceeds. The problem is that synchronous calls between services couple their availability. If Service B is slow, Service A is slow. If Service B is down, Service A fails. In a system with eight to ten agents in a workflow, the cumulative effect of synchronous coupling is a system that is fragile by design.

Production multi-agent systems use an event bus as the communication layer between agents. Kafka is the right choice when you need durability, ordered delivery within partitions, and consumer group semantics that allow multiple agent instances to process work concurrently without duplicate execution. Each agent type has its own topic. The orchestrator publishes task assignments; specialist agents consume from their assigned topics, process work, and publish results to a results topic that the orchestrator monitors.

This architecture decouples agent availability from workflow progress. A specialist agent can be restarted, scaled horizontally, or replaced without affecting the orchestrator's ability to continue processing other tasks. Consumer group offsets mean that work in progress is not lost when an agent pod restarts — it is reprocessed from the last committed offset. That is the difference between a system with recoverable failures and one that requires manual intervention every time a pod evicts.

Failure Mode 3: The Orchestration Logic Lives Inside the LLM

Many agent frameworks encourage a pattern where the LLM decides which tool to call next, in what order, and with what parameters — on every step of every task. This is appropriate for exploratory, open-ended tasks. It is inappropriate for business workflows where the sequence of operations is known, the error handling is defined, and the cost of an incorrect decision is real.

When orchestration logic lives entirely inside an LLM, you cannot unit test it. You cannot trace why a specific decision was made. You cannot enforce that a compliance check always runs before a data write. You cannot guarantee that a retry will follow the same execution path as the original attempt. Every run is a probabilistic event.

Production systems separate orchestration logic from LLM inference. The orchestrator is a deterministic state machine: it knows which agent handles which task type, it enforces sequencing constraints, it manages retries with backoff, and it escalates to human review when confidence thresholds are not met. LLM calls are leaf nodes in the execution graph — they perform specific inference tasks (classification, extraction, generation) and return structured outputs that the deterministic orchestrator acts on. This architecture is testable, traceable, and auditable in a way that pure LLM orchestration is not.

Failure Mode 4: Security Is Added After the Architecture Is Set

Agent systems make external calls: to LLM APIs, to internal databases, to third-party services, to browser automation targets. Each of those calls requires credentials. In prototype systems, credentials are typically environment variables loaded at startup, shared across all agents, and scoped to whatever the developer needed at the time. In production, this is a significant security liability.

Least-privilege IAM means each agent has credentials scoped to exactly the resources it needs and nothing more. A web scraping agent needs outbound HTTP access and write access to a specific S3 bucket or Postgres table. It does not need database admin rights or access to the LLM API keys used by the summarisation agent. When credentials are shared across agents, a compromise of one agent is a compromise of all of them.

In a Kubernetes environment, this is implemented through service accounts with RBAC policies, Kubernetes Secrets mounted as volumes (not environment variables), and — where the infrastructure supports it — workload identity federation that eliminates long-lived credentials entirely. The architecture decision to implement least-privilege IAM from day one is trivial. The decision to retrofit it onto a system where all agents share a single credential set is expensive and disruptive.

Failure Mode 5: There Is No Human Oversight Layer

The organisations that are most cautious about deploying AI agents are often right to be cautious — not because the technology is unreliable, but because the systems they are evaluating have no mechanism for human review before consequential actions execute. An agent that can write to a production database, send emails on behalf of the company, or submit forms to external services needs a configurable approval layer for actions above a defined risk threshold.

This is not a limitation to be engineered around. It is a feature that makes deployment politically viable inside organisations with compliance requirements, legal review processes, or simply leadership teams that are not yet ready to grant autonomous execution rights to a system they do not fully understand. The ability to configure human-in-the-loop checkpoints at specific workflow nodes — and to adjust those thresholds as trust accumulates — is what allows an agent system to start with conservative autonomy and expand it incrementally based on demonstrated reliability.

The technical implementation is straightforward: tasks that reach a review checkpoint are written to a Postgres table with status pending_review, surfaced in an oversight interface, and held until a human approves or rejects them. The agent resumes from the checkpoint on approval. On rejection, the task is marked with the rejection reason and the orchestrator routes it appropriately. The overhead is minimal. The organisational value is significant.

What Production Systems Do Differently: A Summary

  • Durable state from the start. Agent task state lives in Postgres with a schema designed for the orchestration model, not retrofitted to it.
  • Async communication between agents. Kafka topics per agent type, consumer groups for horizontal scaling, offset commits for at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing.
  • Deterministic orchestration with LLM inference at the leaves. The state machine is code. The LLM handles specific inference tasks within that state machine, not the state machine itself.
  • Least-privilege credentials per agent. Kubernetes service accounts, scoped secrets, and workload identity where available. No shared credential sets.
  • Configurable human oversight. Risk-threshold checkpoints at workflow nodes, surfaced in an oversight interface, with approval state tracked in the durable store.

The Architecture Conversation That Should Happen First

Most agent projects that stall do so because the architecture conversation happens too late — after a prototype has been built, after stakeholders have seen a demo and formed expectations, after the team has committed to an approach that will not survive contact with production infrastructure. The decisions described above are not difficult to make. They are difficult to make retroactively
